title: GPX to CSV Converter: Trackpoints to Rows
description: Convert a GPX file to CSV with the GPX to CSV Converter — latitude, longitude, elevation, time and names as spreadsheet columns. Free, local.
summary_sentence: For example, a 2,050-point recording becomes a 2,050-row table whose first row reads 40.7681, −73.9719, the point's elevation, its UTC stamp and its name — the whole track, spreadsheet-legible.
quick_answer: The GPX to CSV Converter opens a GPX file locally and extracts latitude, longitude, elevation, time and names into a simple CSV for spreadsheets and analysis. Load the file and download the table — one row per point, ready for sorting, filtering and charting.

Weather logs, photo times, sensor exports — CSV is the lingua franca every dataset can be joined in, on the timestamp column.
R, pandas, and every BI tool eat CSV natively. The conversion is the on-ramp from a watch's world to an analyst's.
A CSV of the points opens in thirty years of software, past and future — the plainest possible edition of the recording.

examples.label: Example · The header tells the contract

body.t: Columns: latitude, longitude, elevation, time, name — in that order, with latitude and longitude as separate decimal columns (not a fused 'coordinates' string), because tables are for computing and fused strings are for reading.

Trackpoints become rows in sequence — row order is journey order, so a spreadsheet's row number is a proxy for distance along, and sorting by another column is a decision to break that mirror knowingly.

popular_table.note: Blank means absent in the source, never zero — a missing elevation and a sea-level elevation are different facts, and the export refuses to merge them.

faq: Which points are exported — tracks, routes, waypoints?

The export covers the file's points with their type context preserved in the data where the source distinguishes them; trackpoints form the bulk of any recording, route points and waypoints ride with their names doing the identifying.
As recorded: ISO 8601 UTC (…Z). Spreadsheets may display it converted to your zone on import — the value travels correctly; watch the display before accusing the data.
Comma-delimited with standard quoting (RFC 4180 conventions): names containing commas are quoted, so the table parses in Excel, Sheets and pandas identically.
Browser memory bounds the party — a million-row CSV is producible but unwieldy; split epic files first, or let desktop tools (ogr2ogr, GPSBabel) carry industrial loads.
Can the CSV go back to GPX?

Point tables round-trip through the CSV-to-GeoJSON lane for mapping; a full GPX reconstruction needs segment structure the flat table does not promise to keep. Archive the original GPX; export CSVs as working copies.
Metres, as GPX stores them. Convert the column in your spreadsheet if feet are required — a deliberate, visible transformation beats a converter's silent one.
